title: Data Newsroom
tagline: You question a set of data until it gives you a story worth telling.
objectives: Write a rule with a column, a sign and a number or a word, and read how many rows it keeps.
Join two rules with AND, which needs both, or OR, which needs one.
Use BETWEEN to keep every number from one end to the other, both ends in.
Use NOT to keep the rows a rule would leave out.
Say whether the numbers back a headline, and if not, why: too few people, only the best bit, the numbers say no, one did not cause the other.

opening.line1: Today you find out if a headline is telling the truth.
opening.line2: You check it against the facts it came from.
opening.line3: Your feed, adverts and the news tell you things every day. Some are not true.

story.b1: Fionn has gone home sick. Six headlines sit on his desk, unchecked.
story.b2: The paper prints at midnight. Nothing prints without a check.
story.b3: You are the night desk. The facts are in a table. You ask the table questions. Then you stamp each headline: PRINT or SPIKE, do not print.

facts.intro: Fionn put his facts in two tables: grids of rows and columns. Every headline tonight comes from one of them.
facts.t1: 60 people of Rathmore answered a survey.
facts.t1cols: age · area · phone hours · sleep hours · exam score · café visits · pet · bus stars
facts.t2: Table two holds 92 summer days at the harbour.
facts.t2cols: date · temperature · rain · visitors · ice creams sold · sea rescues

tour.s1: This is the table. It has sixty people. Each person is one row.
tour.s2: This is the question box. Type a rule, a question for the table, then press Enter. Rows that fit your rule stay.
tour.s3: This is the count. It tells you how many rows are left.

c1.title: The question
c1.headline: Eight hours of sleep lifts exam scores
c1.show1: A rule has a column, a sign and a number.
c1.show2: age is the column. < means less than. It keeps people under 20.
c1.show3: A rule is also called a query.
c1.ask: Keep only the people who slept eight hours or more.
c1.h1: The column is sleep_hours. The sign for eight or more is >=.
c1.h2: Write the column, then the sign, then the number: sleep_hours, then >=, then 8.

judge.ok: Showing 17 of 60. Seventeen people slept eight hours or more.
judge.wrong: Your rule shows {got} rows, but it should show 17. Check the sign.

options: No. The long sleepers scored lower.
c1.right: Right. The numbers say the opposite.
c1.wrong: Look again. The long sleepers scored lower, not higher.
c1.stampShow2: Dee stamped it SPIKE, meaning do not print.
c1.stampShow3: Her reason: too few people. Every stamp needs one.
c1.stampAsk: Your turn. Stamp it, then pick a reason.
c1.stampOk: SPIKE. The numbers say no: long sleepers 61.0, others 65.3.
c1.stampNo: Look at the two averages. The long sleepers scored lower.
c1.reasonNo: Seventeen people is enough to check. The averages show the headline is wrong.
c1.doneLine: One headline checked. Five are left.
c1.stampShowCard: Harbour café is the town favourite

c2.title: Two at once
c2.headline: Most Rathmore teens are on their phones five hours a day
c2.show1: AND joins two rules. It keeps a row only when both are true.
c2.show2: This keeps teens with a dog: 3 of 60.
c2.show3: Words go in quotes. Numbers do not.
c2.ask: Keep teens who use their phone five hours or more.
c2.h1: Teens: age < 20. Five hours or more: phone_hours >= 5.
c2.h2: Put AND between the two rules.

judge.ok: Showing 6 of 60. Six of the 18 teens use their phone that much.
judge.wrong: Your rule shows {got} rows, but it should show 6. Check both rules.

c2.right: Right. Six of eighteen is one in three.
c2.wrong: Six of eighteen is one in three. That is not most.
c2.stampOk: SPIKE. The numbers say no: 6 of 18 is not most.
c2.stampNo: Only six of the eighteen teens use their phone that much. Is that most?
c2.reasonNo: Eighteen teens is enough to ask. The word "most" is the problem.

c3.title: One week
c3.headline: Rathmore harbour gets 3,000 visitors a day
c3.show1: BETWEEN keeps every number from one end to the other, both ends too.
c3.show2: It keeps days of 20 to 22 degrees: 16 of 92.
c3.show3: Each row here is one summer day.
c3.ask: Fionn only looked at days 40 to 46. Keep those days.
c3.h2: day_no BETWEEN the first day AND the last day.

judge.ok: Showing 7 of 92 days. That is regatta week, the harbour boat races, 10 to 16 July.
judge.wrong: Your rule shows {got} days, but it should show 7. Check both ends.

options: Took the best week and called it the summer.
c3.right: Right. One good week is not the whole summer.
c3.wrong: He took the best week and called it the summer.
c3.stampOk: SPIKE. Only the best bit. Regatta week is not the whole summer.
c3.stampNo: Fionn used seven days out of 92. Can seven days show the whole summer?
c3.reasonNo: The numbers for that week are true. The problem is which week.

c4.title: Either one
c4.headline: More than half of Rathmore people have a dog or a cat
c4.show1: OR keeps a row when either rule is true.
c4.show2: This keeps people in Marsh or Hill: 30 of 60.
c4.show3: Each side of OR is a whole rule: column, sign, number or word.
c4.ask: Keep everyone with a dog or a cat.
c4.h1: The column is pet. Words go in quotes: "dog".
c4.h2: Type pet = "dog" OR pet = "cat". Each side is a full rule.

judge.ok: Showing 31 of 60. That is more than half.
judge.wrong: Your rule shows {got} rows, but it should show 31. Write a full rule on each side of OR.

c4.wrong: Thirty-one of sixty is over half. This one is true.
c4.stampOk: PRINT. The numbers back it: 31 of 60.
c4.stampNo: Not every headline is wrong. 31 of 60 is over half.
c4.reasonNo: This headline is true. The reason to print is that the numbers back it.

c5.title: Leave out
c5.headline: Outside Old Town, everyone loves the new bus
c5.show1: NOT reverses a rule. It keeps everyone the rule would have left out.
c5.show2: This keeps everyone except Old Town: 44 of 60.
c5.show3: NOT sits in front of the rule.
c5.ask: Keep people outside Old Town who gave the bus any stars.
c5.h1: Outside Old Town: NOT area = "Old Town". Any stars: bus_stars > 0.

judge.ok: Showing 4 of 60. Four people rated the bus at all.
judge.wrong: Your rule shows {got} rows, but it should show 4. Put NOT first, then AND.

c5.compare2: The other 40 outside Old Town never rated it.
c5.right: Right. Four people cannot tell us what all 44 think.
c5.wrong: Four people rated it. They cannot tell us what all 44 think.
c5.stampNo: Only four of the 44 people rated the bus. Is that enough for "everyone"?
c5.reasonNo: The four did love it. There are just too few of them.

c6.title: The rush
c6.headline: Ice cream sales cause sea rescues
c6.ring: This is Dee. One headline is left. The press starts in three minutes. If you run out of time, Fionn’s headline prints as it is.
c6.intro: Fionn says more ice creams mean more sea rescues. Check the hot days, then the cold days.
c6.ask1: Keep the hot days: 24 degrees or more.

judge1.ok: Showing 27 of 92. Hot days: 290 ice creams, 2.8 rescues a day.
judge1.wrong: Your rule shows {got} days, but it should show 27. Check the sign.

c6.ask2: Now the cold days: under 18 degrees.

judge2.ok: Showing 28 of 92. Cold days: 91 ice creams, 0.5 rescues a day.
judge2.wrong: Your rule shows {got} days, but it should show 28. Check the sign.

c6.stampOk: SPIKE. One did not cause the other. The heat brings swimmers and ice-cream buyers.
c6.stampNo: Both rise together. Does one cause the other, or does heat cause both?
c6.reasonNo: The numbers are real and there are enough days. What causes what?
c6.timeUp: Midnight. Time is up, so the press printed Fionn’s headline on page one.
c6.printedLine: It printed. Fionn’s headline is on page one.
c6.letter1: Dear Editor, I sell the harbour ice cream.
c6.letter2: Your front page blamed my cones for three rescues.
c6.letter3: Hot days fill the beach with swimmers and my customers.
c6.letter4: The sun did it, not the ice cream. Marie Byrne.
c6.fixAsk: Stamp it again, with the right reason.
c6.fixOk: Corrected. The heat caused both. Nothing is lost.
c6.doneLine: Six headlines checked. The press is running.
c6.compare1: Each hot day: 290 ice creams, 2.8 rescues.
c6.compare2: Each cold day: 91 ice creams, 0.5 rescues.

badges.name: The week
badges.line: BETWEEN kept days in a row.

badges.name: Either one
badges.line: OR: one rule or the other.

recap: A query asks a table a question.
AND needs both. OR needs one.
BETWEEN keeps both ends and all between.
Before you print, ask: enough people? Whole picture? Numbers back it? What caused what?
close.exitWrong: Not that one. The green one is right.

exit.stem: Which rule keeps teens who live in Hill?
Six of 18 teens matched. Eighteen teens is enough to ask. Fionn wrote "most". Why spike it?
options: One did not cause the other

exit.stem: day_no BETWEEN 40 AND 46 keeps how many days?
Hot days bring more ice creams and more rescues. So…
options: Rescued swimmers then buy ice cream

exit.stem: Which rule keeps everyone except Old Town?

felt: I can write a rule with AND, OR or NOT.
I can say what BETWEEN keeps.
I can say why a headline gets spiked.
close.freeIntro: Two more of Fionn’s headlines. Check them with your own rules.

free.headline: Harbour people visit the café most
free.hint: Try area = "Harbour" and read the café average.
free.reveal: Harbour people average 7.9 café visits. Everyone else averages 7.4. Barely different, so Dee spikes it.

free.headline: Rain keeps the visitors away
free.hint: Try rain_mm > 5, then rain_mm = 0. Read the visitors average.
free.reveal: Wet days had 1,846 visitors a day. Dry days had 2,559. The numbers agree, so Dee prints it.
